{{nihongo|'''Atsuhitakahiko Shrine'''|熱日高彦神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} located in {{ill|Kakuda, Miyagi|Q696425|qid=Q696425}}, {{ill|Miyagi Prefecture|Q47896|qid=Q47896}}. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|lt=former shrine rank}}, it was classified as a {{ill|Gō-sha|Q134917316|qid=Q134917316}}. It is a {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932|lt=shrine listed in the Engishiki}} and also serves as the {{ill|Sōja shrine|Q1107129|qid=Q1107129|lt=general shrine}} of {{ill|Igu District, Miyagi|Q1155531|qid=Q1155531}}. {{nihongo|'''Atsuhitakahiko Shrine'''|熱日高彦神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Mutsu Province]].

== Enshrined deities ==
* {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|Q1056017|qid=Q1056017|lt=Amatsuhidaka Hikonohono Ninigi no Mikoto}}, {{ill|Yamato Takeru|Q461258|qid=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru no Mikoto}}
** In addition, the shrine also jointly enshrines Susanoo no Mikoto, Shiotsuchi no Oji no Mikoto, Ōnamuchi no Kami, Sukunahikona no Mikoto, and the deities of nearby shrines such as Shirayama Shrine, Kumano Shrine, Suijin Shrine, and Tachi Inari Shrine.

== History ==
According to shrine tradition, Yamato Takeru, a son of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|Q329723|qid=Q329723}}, was ordered by imperial command to head east. On his journey, he reached the land of Igu and established a ritual site at the foot of Mount Ōmori, an ancient sacred place, where he enshrined Ninigi no Mikoto, the ancestral deity of the Yamato imperial court. Afterward, Yamato Takeru set out on his return to the capital, but upon his death, Emperor Keikō, in remembrance of his son’s achievements, ordered the construction of a shrine building and enshrined Yamato Takeru together with Ninigi no Mikoto.

In the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}, Atsuhitakahiko Shrine was listed as one of the hundred Shikinaisha in Mutsu Province. According to the Igu District Gazetteer, the sacred object of Atsuhitakahiko Shrine is said to be a bronze Buddhist statue cast at Nyoiji Temple in Yamashiro Province by order of {{ill|Emperor Daigo|Q329753|qid=Q329753|lt=the Engi Emperor}}. During the Edo period, Atsuhitakahiko Shrine was regarded as the sōsha of Igu District. About 4 km west of the shrine are the ruins of the Igu District government office, known as the Kōriyama archaeological site. In the 5th year of the {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} era (1872), it was designated the only gōsha within Igu District.

At the spring grand festival, in the past, the portable shrines (mikoshi) of Kashima Shrine in Kosai, Marumori Town (enshrining {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi|Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi no Kami}}), and Katori Shrine in the Ōyama-Ōtani area of Kakuda City (enshrining {{ill|Futsunushi|fr|Futsunushi|it|Futsunushi|ja|経津主神|mni|ꯐꯨꯠꯁꯨꯅꯨꯁꯤ|pl|Futsunushi|ru|Фуцунуси|zh|經津主神|qid=Q1107286|lt=Futsunushi no Kami}}) would gather at Atsuhitakahiko Shrine, and the three mikoshi would proceed together in a joint procession. At present, the procession is held jointly with the mikoshi of Katori Shrine only.

<gallery widths="200px" heights="150px">
File:Haiden of Katori-jinja shrine.JPG|Ōtani Katori Shrine
File:Haiden of Kosai Kashima-jinja shrine.JPG|Kosai Kashima Shrine
</gallery>

Atsuhitakahiko Shrine is revered as a shrine bestowing divine blessings for fertility and childrearing, martial arts and politics, fire prevention, agriculture, and traffic safety.
